items_missed: No real agenda statement. 'We can talk to the details a little bit, just make sure that's good on our end, answer any questions you might have' is a gesture at a roadmap but carries no pricing sequence, no 10–15 minute timeframe, and no confirmation ask — and the call then ran 19 minutes.
No 'sound good?' confirmation at the open.
Never asked 'how are you today?' — went straight from the greeting into pulling up the record.

Clock section is a complete zero. No 'your time starts when the crew arrives,' no two-and-a-half hour minimum, no fifteen-minute prorated increments, no sense-check. The customer walked away believing billing floats freely downward — 'the less I have the less time it takes and the price will just go down' — with no floor and no increment granularity ever stated. See the live-risk note.
No 'pricing is super simple' framing. Pricing never got its own moment; it emerged in fragments buried inside inventory talk.

Per-mover rate never stated. He led with totals ($1,635, then $1,427, then $1,560) and only surfaced 'the hourly rate of $208' after the customer repeated a number back to him — she was never told it is $104 per mover per hour with a two-man crew.
Inclusions list incomplete — blankets, shrink wrap, and truck were covered, but no gas, no taxes, no insurance, no tools/equipment.

Disassembly and reassembly never confirmed as included, despite being asked directly and twice. 'I need somebody who's going to be able to put the beds together, who's going to be able to unhook and hook up the washer and dryer and all that kind of good stuff' drew 'Gotcha. And then for the box count...' — he pivoted to boxes and never came back to it.

Her stated main concern was never addressed. She named the 60-inch TV as her worry twice ('my main concern would be moving the sixty inch,' then 'the sixty inch that I'm more concerned with') and got 'Mm-hmm yeah, that's the.' No TV box, no crating, no wrap protocol, no reassurance.

Moving-stressor question never asked — and she volunteered the underlying one anyway ('I'm a little bit older now and so I really need somebody who's gonna do all of it'), which was never reflected back or built on.

Packing service never quoted. She twice signaled she may not finish packing and needs full service, and the answer was 'let us know' rather than 'packing runs at the same hourly rate plus materials — want me to price that as a contingency?'
Meet Your Mover never mentioned. The morning ETA call is not a substitute.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — and he gave an 8:45–9:15 arrival window and blamed traffic for the variance, which is precisely the setup for it.
No 'no hidden fees' pitch.
'No deposit required' never mentioned — on a price-shopper who said outright she was going to compare quotes.
Email handoff never explained. No confirmation email was ever promised. 'Give us an email or phone call' if things change is the opposite direction of travel.
No BOLDED-details framing and no 'reply with any corrections.'
Business hours never given.
No equivalents or volume reference used to help her picture why 4.5 system hours became 7.5.
Ecobox referral missed on a customer self-packing 25–40 boxes.
Customer's name used once in 19 minutes ('Robin, do you have any other questions...') — short of the 3+ standard.

Inventory-gathering ran long and unmanaged. He let her count small furniture out loud at length ('1234 567891 01112... 131415') without steering, and the pricing readout that followed was hard to follow ('so for the full seven and a half, that'd be 1635 if it took full seven and a half, closer to six and a half would be the 1427'), producing three different totals in under a minute.
top_strength: This is the estimate-accuracy behavior we have been asking for, done unprompted and out loud. Daniel looked at the system's number and overrode it with reasoning: 'for what you had on here, I think they had you like four and a half hours — I think that is a little bit under doing it. Two bedrooms are a little bit sneaky especially with how much stuff you can fit in there... I think the system kinda under does for the third floor stairs and then washer/dryer, it didn't factor in that time, which I would probably at least thirty minutes for that sort of thing.' He then rebuilt it bottom-up into 4–5 hours of loading plus 2–2.5 unloading and landed at 6.5–7.5, and the customer accepted it immediately because the logic was visible ('that's reasonable, I was putting you guys probably somewhere around 1500'). His probing was the other standout — the best in this batch — working the third-floor exterior stairs, truck-to-stairs walk distance, the side-door parking workaround, the balcony closet, the attached shed at the destination, glass and marble tops, and a piece-by-piece furniture list, all with an explicit reason given for the detail: 'any additional pieces, additional trips back and forth from the stairs, so it's always good to kind of get an accurate list.' He also handled a real objection without a trace of defensiveness — when she said she needed 'more of an established company than you guys off the street,' he answered 'even the workers with us, we also didn't get them off the street. They're all hired and trained in-house, they're background checked employees,' and she softened for the rest of the call.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: you gave zero clock explanation on a $1,560 job, so she is now operating on a belief you left uncorrected — that the price only moves down. Say it plainly and early: 'Your time starts when the crew arrives on site and opens the contract, there's a two-and-a-half hour minimum, and past that we bill in fifteen-minute prorated increments, so you only pay for the time you actually use. Does that make sense?' Second priority: Robin asked you twice whether your crew assembles beds and hooks up the washer and dryer, and both times you moved on to box counts — answer the thing she is actually buying on ('Yes, disassembly and reassembly are included in the hourly rate, and the crew will handle the washer and dryer'), and resolve the 60-inch TV she named as her main concern instead of humming past it, because an unanswered worry is what sends a self-described price-shopper to the next quote. Third, you earned the booking and never secured it — no deposit mention, no confirmation email, no 'reply with any corrections'; those three lines cost fifteen seconds and are what make a hesitant buyer stop shopping. LIVE BUSINESS RISK: you verbally rewrote the system's 4.5-hour estimate up to 6.5–7.5 hours, restated the total as $1,560, and waived the $75 Round Rock trip fee — and you never promised a confirmation email or said you would update the record. If the crew or the invoice works off the old EMMA figures, this is a billing dispute on move day on a job the customer has already repeated back to you as '1560 for seven and a half hours.' Confirm the revised hours, the revised total, and the waived trip fee are all in EMMA today, and get them to her in writing. SECOND RISK: she is booked for October 15 and there was live date confusion at the end ('the fourteenth?' / 'we're on the fifteenth') on a date you first read aloud as 'the eighteenth' — worth verifying the scheduled date is right. DATA NOTE for the roster: the Dialpad record labels this customer 'Faith Gutman' but she identifies herself as Robin Gutman and Daniel calls her Robin throughout — another instance of the name-mismatch issue, and it will affect the phone-number join.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and collaborative — he affirmed her generously and naturally ('You are exactly right,' 'I appreciate you walking through that,' 'those are, oh, there's always one'), absorbed a pointed objection about hiring 'off the street' without getting defensive, and moved her from open price-shopping to 'that's perfect' by the end; held back from a 5 by missing both worries she stated out loud (the 60-inch TV and needing full service because she is older) and by a rambling delivery that used her name only once in nineteen minutes.
